rows.stem: The roots of the quadratic equation \((x - 1)^2 = 16\) are :

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the given figure, PQ and PR are tangents to a circle with centre O and radius 3 cm. If \(\angle QPR = 60^\circ\), then the length of each tangent is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with centre O, the tangents PQ and PR and the radii OQ and OR, with the angle at P marked; the stem states every value. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The radius OQ is perpendicular to the tangent PQ, so \(\angle OQP = 90^\circ\). OP bisects the angle between the two tangents, so \(\angle OPQ = 30^\circ\).

In right triangle OQP: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{OQ}{PQ}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{3}{PQ}\) and \(PQ = 3\sqrt{3}\) cm.

This is option (A) \(3\sqrt{3}\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Basic Proportionality Theorem
rows.stem: In \(\Delta DEF\), \(AB \parallel EF\). The value of x is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the lengths DA, AE, DB and BF (in terms of x) are given only as labels on the drawing. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
In the figure \(DA = 2x\), \(AE = 3x + 1\), \(DB = x\) and \(BF = 2x - \dfrac{1}{2}\). Since \(AB \parallel EF\), the Basic Proportionality Theorem gives \(\dfrac{DA}{AE} = \dfrac{DB}{BF}\):

\(\dfrac{2x}{3x + 1} = \dfrac{x}{2x - \frac{1}{2}}\), so \(2x\left(2x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = x(3x + 1)\), that is \(4x^2 - x = 3x^2 + x\) and \(x^2 - 2x = 0\).

So \(x = 0\) or \(x = 2\). A length cannot be zero (DB would vanish), so \(x = 2\), which is option (B) \(2\) only.

rows.subtopic: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
rows.stem: \((3 \times 11 \times 13 + 3)\) is :
rows.solution:
\(3 \times 11 \times 13 + 3 = 3(11 \times 13 + 1) = 3 \times 144 = 432\).

The number has the factor 3 besides 1 and itself, so it is composite. (432 is even, and \(432 = 13 \times 33 + 3\) is not a multiple of 13.)

This is option (C) a composite number.

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Two dice are rolled together. The probability that the sum of the numbers obtained is divisible by 6, is :
rows.solution:
Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, a sum of 6 comes from (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), (4, 2), (5, 1), and a sum of 12 from (6, 6). That is 6 outcomes.

\(P = \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}\), which is option (A) \(\dfrac{1}{6}\).

rows.subtopic: nth Term of an AP
rows.stem: The number of multiples of 4 lying between 12 and 250 is :
rows.solution:
The multiples of 4 between 12 and 250 are \(16, 20, 24, \ldots, 248\), an AP with \(a = 16\), \(d = 4\) and last term 248.

\(248 = 16 + (n - 1) \times 4\) gives \(n - 1 = 58\), so \(n = 59\).

This is option (A) \(59\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A cone of maximum size is carved out from a solid cube of edge length \(l\). The volume of the cone is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a cube with an inverted cone drawn inside it, its base on the top face; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The largest cone has its base on one face of the cube and its vertex on the opposite face, so its radius is \(\dfrac{l}{2}\) and its height is \(l\).

Volume \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right)^2 l = \dfrac{\pi l^3}{12}\), which is option (A) \(\dfrac{\pi l^3}{12}\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: Equation of another line parallel to the line represented by \(2x - 6y = 7\) is :
rows.solution:
For \(2x - 6y = 7\) and \(x - 3y = 7\): \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{2}{1}\), \(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-6}{-3} = 2\) and \(\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{7}{7} = 1\).

\(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), so the two lines are parallel. (The lines \(2x + 6y = 9\) and \(x + 3y = \dfrac{7}{2}\) slope the other way, and \(y = 3x - 7\) has slope 3, not \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).)

This is option (C) \(x - 3y = 7\).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: If the length of the shadow of a tower is \(\sqrt{3}\) times that of its height, then altitude of the Sun is :
rows.solution:
Let the height of the tower be h, so its shadow is \(\sqrt{3}\,h\). If \(\theta\) is the altitude of the Sun,

\(\tan\theta = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}\,h} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(\theta = 30^\circ\), which is option (B) \(30^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: If the roots of the quadratic equation \(\sqrt{3}x^2 - kx + 2\sqrt{3} = 0\) are real and equal, then the value(s) of k is/are :
rows.solution:
Real and equal roots need the discriminant to be zero:

\(k^2 - 4 \times \sqrt{3} \times 2\sqrt{3} = 0\), that is \(k^2 - 24 = 0\), so \(k = \pm\sqrt{24}\).

This is option (A) \(\pm\sqrt{24}\).

rows.subtopic: nth Term of an AP
rows.stem: The \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the A.P. \(\dfrac{-1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{5}{3}, \dfrac{8}{3}, \ldots\) is :
rows.solution:
Here \(a = -\dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(d = \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = 1\).

\(a_n = a + (n - 1)d = -\dfrac{1}{3} + n - 1 = n - \dfrac{4}{3}\), which is option (B) \(n - \dfrac{4}{3}\).

rows.subtopic: Tangent to a Circle
rows.stem: In the given figure, PT is a tangent to the circle with centre O and radius r. If \(\angle POT = 45^\circ\), then the length of OP is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with centre O, the tangent PT and the radius OT marked r, with the angle at O marked; the stem states every value. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent PT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T.

\(\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{OT}{OP}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{r}{OP}\) and \(OP = r\sqrt{2}\).

This is option (A) \(r\sqrt{2}\).

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: It is given that \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta QRP\) such that AB = 9 cm, BC = 5 cm and PR = 2 cm. Length of side QR is :
rows.solution:
\(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta QRP\) matches A with Q, B with R and C with P, so \(\dfrac{AB}{QR} = \dfrac{BC}{RP}\).

\(\dfrac{9}{QR} = \dfrac{5}{2}\) gives \(QR = \dfrac{18}{5} = 3{\cdot}6\) cm, which is option (D) \(3{\cdot}6\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: The sum and product of zeroes of a quadratic polynomial \(p(x)\) are \(\dfrac{-1}{3}\) and 2 respectively. The polynomial \(p(x)\) is :
rows.solution:
A quadratic with sum of zeroes \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\) and product 2 is a multiple of \(x^2 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)x + 2 = x^2 + \dfrac{1}{3}x + 2\).

Multiplying by \(-3\) gives \(-3x^2 - x - 6\). (Check: sum \(= -\dfrac{-1}{-3} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\), product \(= \dfrac{-6}{-3} = 2\).)

This is option (D) \(-3x^2 - x - 6\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of Specific Angles
rows.stem: Given that \(\sin 2\alpha = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), the value of \(\sin 3\alpha\) is :
rows.solution:
\(\sin 2\alpha = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) gives \(2\alpha = 60^\circ\) (an acute angle), so \(\alpha = 30^\circ\).

\(\sin 3\alpha = \sin 90^\circ = 1\), which is option (C) \(1\).

rows.subtopic: Median of Grouped Data
rows.stem: The median and mode of a distribution are \(25{\cdot}2\) and \(26{\cdot}1\) respectively. The mean of the distribution is :
rows.solution:
Use the empirical relation Mode \(= 3\,\)Median \(- 2\,\)Mean:

\(26{\cdot}1 = 3 \times 25{\cdot}2 - 2\,\text{Mean} = 75{\cdot}6 - 2\,\text{Mean}\), so \(2\,\text{Mean} = 49{\cdot}5\) and Mean \(= 24{\cdot}75\).

This is option (A) \(24{\cdot}75\).

rows.subtopic: Distance Formula
rows.stem: In the given figure, \(\Delta ABC\) is an equilateral triangle. AD is a median of the triangle joining the points \(A\left(0, \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\), \(D(0, 0)\). Points B and C are (in same order) :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - which of B and C lies on which side of D along the x-axis is fixed only by the drawing, and the question asks for B and C in that order. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
In an equilateral triangle of side a, the median AD is also the altitude, of length \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a\).

\(AD = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(a = 5\). D is the mid-point of BC, so \(BD = DC = \dfrac{5}{2}\), with BC along the x-axis.

In the figure B lies to the left of D and C to the right, so B is \(\left(-\dfrac{5}{2}, 0\right)\) and C is \(\left(\dfrac{5}{2}, 0\right)\).

This is option (B) \(\left(-\dfrac{5}{2}, 0\right), \left(\dfrac{5}{2}, 0\right)\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of Specific Angles
rows.stem: The value of \(\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\tan^2 45^\circ - \cos^2 60^\circ\right)\) is :
rows.solution:
\(\tan 45^\circ = 1\) and \(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 1^2 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\), which is option (C) \(\dfrac{1}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Tangent to a Circle
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Radius is the smallest distance of a tangent from the centre of the circle.

**Reason (R) :** Radius is perpendicular to the tangent.
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent, so the Reason is true.

The shortest distance from a point to a line is along the perpendicular. So the shortest distance from the centre to the tangent is the radius drawn to the point of contact, and the Assertion is true. The Assertion follows directly from the Reason.

Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of Specific Angles
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** \(\tan 2\theta\) is not defined at \(\theta = 45^\circ\).

**Reason (R) :** \(\sin 90^\circ \neq \cos 90^\circ\).
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
At \(\theta = 45^\circ\), \(\tan 2\theta = \tan 90^\circ = \dfrac{\sin 90^\circ}{\cos 90^\circ} = \dfrac{1}{0}\), which is not defined. The Assertion is true.

\(\sin 90^\circ = 1\) and \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), so \(\sin 90^\circ \neq \cos 90^\circ\), and the Reason is true. But \(\tan 90^\circ\) is undefined because \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), not because the sine and cosine differ (they differ at \(60^\circ\) too, where the tangent is defined). So the Reason does not explain the Assertion.

Both statements are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the length of the plank that can be used to measure the lengths 4 m 20 cm and 5 m 4 cm exactly, in the least time.
rows.solution:
4 m 20 cm \(= 420\) cm and 5 m 4 cm \(= 504\) cm.

To measure both lengths exactly in the least time, the plank must be as long as possible while dividing both lengths exactly, so its length is the HCF of 420 and 504.

\(420 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7\) and \(504 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 7\), so HCF \(= 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84\).

The required length of the plank is 84 cm.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: In an A.P., the first term is 32 and the last term is \(-10\). If the common difference is \(-2\), then find the number of terms and their sum.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: Find the sum of the first 28 terms of an A.P. whose \(n^{\text{th}}\) term is given by \(a_n = 3n - 2\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem:
Diagonals AC and BD of square ABCD intersect at P. Coordinates of points B and D are \((9, -2)\) and \((1, 6)\) respectively.

(i) Find the co-ordinates of point P.

(ii) Find the length of the side of the square.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the square ABCD with its diagonals meeting at P and the coordinates of D and B marked; the stem states every value. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(i) The diagonals of a square bisect each other, so P is the mid-point of BD:

\(P = \left(\dfrac{9 + 1}{2}, \dfrac{-2 + 6}{2}\right) = (5, 2)\).

(ii) In a square of side AB, the diagonal satisfies \(BD^2 = AB^2 + AD^2 = 2AB^2\).

\(BD^2 = (9 - 1)^2 + (-2 - 6)^2 = 64 + 64 = 128\), so \(2AB^2 = 128\), \(AB^2 = 64\) and \(AB = 8\).

The side of the square is 8 units.

rows.subtopic: Distance Formula
rows.stem: Find the coordinates of a point on the line \(x + y = 5\) which is equidistant from \((6, 4)\) and \((5, 2)\).
rows.solution:
Let the required point be \((x, y)\). It is equidistant from \((6, 4)\) and \((5, 2)\), so

\((6 - x)^2 + (4 - y)^2 = (5 - x)^2 + (2 - y)^2\)

\(36 - 12x + x^2 + 16 - 8y + y^2 = 25 - 10x + x^2 + 4 - 4y + y^2\)

\(52 - 12x - 8y = 29 - 10x - 4y\), that is \(2x + 4y = 23\) ... (i)

The point lies on the line, so \(x + y = 5\) ... (ii)

From (ii), \(x = 5 - y\). Substituting in (i): \(10 - 2y + 4y = 23\), so \(y = \dfrac{13}{2}\) and \(x = -\dfrac{3}{2}\).

The required point is \(\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{13}{2}\right)\).

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: The diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD intersect each other at the point O such that \(\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{BO}{OD}\). Show that quadrilateral ABCD is a trapezium.
rows.solution:
In triangles AOB and COD:

\(\dfrac{AO}{OC} = \dfrac{BO}{OD}\) (given), and \(\angle AOB = \angle COD\) (vertically opposite angles).

So \(\Delta AOB \sim \Delta COD\) (SAS similarity), and their corresponding angles are equal: \(\angle OAB = \angle OCD\).

These are alternate angles made by the transversal AC with the lines AB and DC, so \(AB \parallel DC\).

One pair of opposite sides is parallel, so ABCD is a trapezium.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A toy is in the form of a cone mounted on a hemisphere of radius 7 cm. The total height of the toy is 31 cm. Find the total surface area of the toy.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a cone standing on a hemisphere, with the cone's axis drawn; every value is in the stem. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Height of the conical part \(= 31 - 7 = 24\) cm, and its radius is 7 cm.

Slant height \(l = \sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25\) cm.

Total surface area of the toy \(=\) curved surface of the cone \(+\) curved surface of the hemisphere

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 + 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7 = 550 + 308 = 858\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: If \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\), then prove that \(\tan\theta + \cot\theta = 1\)
rows.solution:
Squaring both sides of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\):

\(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 3\)

\(1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 3\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = 1\) ... (i)

LHS \(= \tan\theta + \cot\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\)

\(= 1\) (using (i)) \(=\) RHS.

Note that no real angle satisfies the given condition, since \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta \le \sqrt{2}\) for every angle.

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: Prove that : \((\sin A + \sec A)^2 + (\cos A + \operatorname{cosec} A)^2 = (1 + \sec A \operatorname{cosec} A)^2\)
rows.solution:
LHS \(= \left(\sin A + \dfrac{1}{\cos A}\right)^2 + \left(\cos A + \dfrac{1}{\sin A}\right)^2\)

\(= \sin^2 A + \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A} + \dfrac{2\sin A}{\cos A} + \cos^2 A + \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A} + \dfrac{2\cos A}{\sin A}\)

\(= 1 + \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin^2 A} + \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A}\right) + 2\left(\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos A} + \dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}\right)\)

\(= 1 + \dfrac{\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A}{\sin^2 A\cos^2 A} + 2 \times \dfrac{\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A}{\sin A\cos A} = 1 + \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 A\sin^2 A} + \dfrac{2}{\cos A\sin A}\)

\(= 1 + \sec^2 A\operatorname{cosec}^2 A + 2\sec A\operatorname{cosec} A = (1 + \sec A\operatorname{cosec} A)^2 =\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Area of a Segment
rows.stem: In the given figure, chord AB subtends an angle of \(120^\circ\) at the centre of the circle with radius 7 cm. Find (i) perimeter of major sector OACB, and (ii) area of the shaded segment, if area of \(\Delta OAB = 21{\cdot}2\,\text{cm}^2\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the point C that names the major sector OACB, and which segment is shaded, are shown only in the drawing. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(i) The major sector OACB has angle \(360^\circ - 120^\circ = 240^\circ\).

Perimeter of the major sector \(=\) length of the major arc ACB \(+ 2 \times\) radius

\(= \dfrac{240}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 + 2 \times 7 = \dfrac{88}{3} + 14 = \dfrac{130}{3}\) cm \(\approx 43{\cdot}33\) cm.

(ii) The shaded segment is the minor segment cut off by the chord AB.

Area of the shaded segment \(=\) area of the minor sector OAB \(-\) area of \(\Delta OAB\)

\(= \dfrac{120}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7 - 21{\cdot}2 = \dfrac{154}{3} - 21{\cdot}2 \approx 51{\cdot}33 - 21{\cdot}2 = 30{\cdot}13\ \text{cm}^2\).

The area of the shaded segment is about \(30{\cdot}1\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: Find two consecutive negative integers, sum of whose squares is 481.
rows.solution:
Let the two consecutive negative integers be x and \(x + 1\).

\(x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 481\) gives \(2x^2 + 2x + 1 = 481\), so \(x^2 + x - 240 = 0\).

\((x + 16)(x - 15) = 0\), so \(x = -16\) or \(x = 15\). The integers must be negative, so \(x = 15\) is rejected and \(x = -16\).

The required integers are \(-16\) and \(-15\). (Check: \(256 + 225 = 481\).)

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: A point \(P(x, 7)\) divides a line segment joining the points \(A(-5, 4)\) and \(B(7, 9)\) in a certain ratio. Find the ratio and hence find the value of x.
rows.solution:
Let P divide AB in the ratio \(AP : PB = k : 1\). Comparing the y-coordinates:

\(7 = \dfrac{9k + 4}{k + 1}\), so \(7k + 7 = 9k + 4\) and \(k = \dfrac{3}{2}\).

The required ratio is \(3 : 2\).

Then \(x = \dfrac{3 \times 7 + 2 \times (-5)}{3 + 2} = \dfrac{21 - 10}{5} = \dfrac{11}{5}\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: Two tangents PA and PB are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point P. Prove that \(\angle APB = 2\angle OAB\).
rows.solution:
The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent AP, so \(\angle OAP = 90^\circ\) and

\(\angle PAB = 90^\circ - \angle OAB\) ... (i)

Tangents from an external point are equal, so \(PA = PB\), and in triangle PAB, \(\angle PAB = \angle PBA\).

The angles of triangle PAB add up to \(180^\circ\), so \(\angle APB = 180^\circ - 2\angle PAB\).

Using (i), \(\angle APB = 180^\circ - 2(90^\circ - \angle OAB) = 2\angle OAB\).

rows.subtopic: Tangent to a Circle
rows.stem: In the given figure, PA is the tangent to the circle with centre O such that OA = 10 cm, AB = 8 cm and \(AB \perp OP\). Find the length of PB.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that A lies on the circle and B lies on the segment OP (inside the circle), with the right angle marked at B, is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
In right triangle OBA (right-angled at B): \(OB = \sqrt{OA^2 - AB^2} = \sqrt{10^2 - 8^2} = 6\) cm.

Let \(\angle AOB = \theta\). Then \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{AB}{OB} = \dfrac{8}{6}\) ... (i)

The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent PA, so triangle OAP is right-angled at A, and \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{AP}{OA} = \dfrac{AP}{10}\).

Using (i), \(\dfrac{AP}{10} = \dfrac{8}{6}\), so \(AP = \dfrac{40}{3}\) cm.

\(OP = \sqrt{AP^2 + OA^2} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{40}{3}\right)^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1600 + 900}{9}} = \dfrac{50}{3}\) cm.

\(PB = OP - OB = \dfrac{50}{3} - 6 = \dfrac{32}{3}\) cm \(\approx 10{\cdot}67\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Basic Proportionality Theorem
rows.stem: In \(\Delta ABC\), AD is a median. X is a point on AD such that \(AX : XD = 2 : 3\). BX is extended so that it intersects AC at Y. Prove that \(BX = 4\,XY\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - triangle ABC with the median AD, the point X on AD and BX extended to meet AC at Y, with BD and DC marked equal; the stem states the configuration in full. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Through D draw \(DZ \parallel BY\), meeting AC at Z.

In triangle CBY, \(DZ \parallel BY\), so \(\dfrac{CD}{DB} = \dfrac{CZ}{ZY} = 1\), since D is the mid-point of BC. Triangles CDZ and CBY are similar (AA), so \(\dfrac{DZ}{BY} = \dfrac{CD}{CB} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), that is \(DZ = \dfrac{1}{2}BY\) ... (i)

In triangle ADZ, \(XY \parallel DZ\) (XY lies along BY). So \(\Delta AXY \sim \Delta ADZ\) (AA), and

\(\dfrac{AX}{AD} = \dfrac{XY}{DZ}\). Since \(AX : XD = 2 : 3\), \(\dfrac{AX}{AD} = \dfrac{2}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{2}{5}\), so \(\dfrac{XY}{DZ} = \dfrac{2}{5}\), or \(DZ = \dfrac{5}{2}XY\) ... (ii)

From (i) and (ii), \(\dfrac{1}{2}BY = \dfrac{5}{2}XY\), so \(BY = 5\,XY\).

Therefore \(BX = BY - XY = 5\,XY - XY = 4\,XY\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem:
Solve the following system of equations graphically :

\(x - 2y = 3, \quad 3x - 8y = 7\)
rows.solution:
Points on \(x - 2y = 3\):

| \(x\) | 1 | 3 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | \(-1\) | 0 | 1 |

Points on \(3x - 8y = 7\):

| \(x\) | \(-3\) | 1 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | \(-2\) | \(-0{\cdot}5\) | 1 |

Plot both sets of points on the same axes and draw the two lines. They meet at the point \((5, 1)\).

The solution is \(x = 5\), \(y = 1\). (Check: \(5 - 2 = 3\) and \(15 - 8 = 7\).)

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem:
Five years ago, Adil was thrice as old as Bharat. Ten years later Adil shall be twice as old as Bharat. To know the present ages of Adil and Bharat :

(i) form the linear equations representing the above information.

(ii) show that the system of equations is consistent with unique solution.

(iii) find the present ages of Adil and Bharat.
rows.solution:
Let the present ages of Adil and Bharat be x years and y years.

(i) Five years ago: \(x - 5 = 3(y - 5)\), that is \(x - 3y = -10\) ... (1)

Ten years later: \(x + 10 = 2(y + 10)\), that is \(x - 2y = 10\) ... (2)

(ii) Here \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1\) and \(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-3}{-2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). Since \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), the lines intersect in exactly one point, so the system is consistent with a unique solution.

(iii) Subtracting (1) from (2): \(y = 20\). Then \(x = 10 + 2y = 50\).

Adil is 50 years old and Bharat is 20 years old. (Check: five years ago 45 and 15; ten years later 60 and 30.)

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: A boy standing on a horizontal plane is flying a kite with a string of length 60 m, at an angle of elevation of \(30^\circ\). Another boy standing on the roof of a 20 m high building, finds the angle of elevation of same kite to be \(45^\circ\). If both the boys are on opposite sides of the kite, find the distance of the first boy from the base of the building. Also, find the height of the kite from the ground. (Use \(\sqrt{3} = 1{\cdot}73\))
rows.solution:
Let K be the kite and P the point on the ground directly below it. Let B be the first boy, on the ground, and let CM be the 20 m building, with C its base and the second boy at M on the roof. Draw ML horizontal to meet KP at L, so \(LP = MC = 20\) m and \(CP = ML\). Let \(KL = h\), \(CP = x\) and \(PB = y\).

In right triangle KPB, with the string \(KB = 60\) m:

\(\dfrac{h + 20}{60} = \sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(h + 20 = 30\) and \(h = 10\).

\(\dfrac{y}{60} = \cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(y = 30\sqrt{3} = 30 \times 1{\cdot}73 = 51{\cdot}9\).

In right triangle KLM: \(\dfrac{KL}{ML} = \tan 45^\circ = 1\), so \(\dfrac{10}{x} = 1\) and \(x = 10\).

Height of the kite from the ground \(= h + 20 = 10 + 20 = 30\) m.

The boys are on opposite sides of the kite, so the distance of the first boy from the base of the building is \(CP + PB = 10 + 51{\cdot}9 = 61{\cdot}9\) m.

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Determine the height of the arch.
rows.context:
During a theatre drama, a backdrop of building arches was used. The shape of the curve shown below can be represented by the polynomial \(p(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 8\), where x is the length (in feet) on stage level.

Based on the figure given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the graph of the arch on the X and Y axes, with the top point labelled C(1, y) and the floor points labelled B and A; p(x) is given in the passage. The photograph of three stage arches beside it is decorative. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
The top of the arch is the point \(C(1, y)\) on the graph, so its height is \(p(1)\):

\(p(1) = -(1)^2 + 2 \times 1 + 8 = 9\).

The height of the arch is 9 feet. (Since \(p(x) = 9 - (x - 1)^2\), 9 is the largest value p takes.)

The drawing shows a round-topped arch with straight sides rather than a parabola; the passage says only that the shape can be represented by \(p(x)\), so the height is read from \(p(x)\).

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Find zeroes of the polynomial \(p(x)\). Which points on the graph represent the zeroes ?
rows.context:
During a theatre drama, a backdrop of building arches was used. The shape of the curve shown below can be represented by the polynomial \(p(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 8\), where x is the length (in feet) on stage level.

Based on the figure given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the question asks which points on the graph represent the zeroes, and the points are named only on the drawing. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
\(p(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 8 = -(x^2 - 2x - 8) = -(x - 4)(x + 2)\).

So the zeroes of \(p(x)\) are \(-2\) and \(4\).

The zeroes are where the curve meets the x-axis: the points B\((-2, 0)\) and A\((4, 0)\) on the graph represent them.

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Find the span of the arch on the stage floor.
rows.context:
During a theatre drama, a backdrop of building arches was used. The shape of the curve shown below can be represented by the polynomial \(p(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 8\), where x is the length (in feet) on stage level.

Based on the figure given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the graph of the arch with the floor points labelled B and A; the span follows from p(x) in the passage. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
\(p(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 8 = -(x - 4)(x + 2)\), so the zeroes are \(-2\) and \(4\).

The arch meets the stage floor (the x-axis) at A\((4, 0)\) and B\((-2, 0)\).

Span of the arch on the stage floor \(= AB = 4 - (-2) = 6\) feet.

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Write the coordinates of the point of intersection of the above curve with the y-axis.
rows.context:
During a theatre drama, a backdrop of building arches was used. The shape of the curve shown below can be represented by the polynomial \(p(x) = -x^2 + 2x + 8\), where x is the length (in feet) on stage level.

Based on the figure given above, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the graph of the arch crossing the Y axis; p(x) is given in the passage. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
On the y-axis \(x = 0\), and \(p(0) = -(0)^2 + 2 \times 0 + 8 = 8\).

The curve meets the y-axis at \((0, 8)\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Find the probability that the drawn card is a face card.
rows.context: A group of friends wanted to play cards with two identical packs together. While shuffling the cards, three cards are dropped. Rest of the cards are shuffled and one card is drawn at random. Assuming that the dropped cards were a queen of hearts, a ten of spades and an ace of clubs, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: DECORATIVE - a photograph of an open wooden box holding two packs of playing cards; every number is in the passage. Page idx 24.
rows.solution:
Two packs hold \(2 \times 52 = 104\) cards. Three are dropped, so \(104 - 3 = 101\) cards remain.

The two packs have \(2 \times 12 = 24\) face cards. Of the dropped cards only the queen of hearts is a face card, so 23 face cards remain.

\(P(\text{face card}) = \dfrac{23}{101}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Find the probability that the drawn card is either a king or a queen.
rows.context: A group of friends wanted to play cards with two identical packs together. While shuffling the cards, three cards are dropped. Rest of the cards are shuffled and one card is drawn at random. Assuming that the dropped cards were a queen of hearts, a ten of spades and an ace of clubs, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Two packs hold \(2 \times 52 = 104\) cards, and after three are dropped 101 remain.

The two packs have 8 kings and 8 queens. The queen of hearts was dropped, so 8 kings and 7 queens remain: 15 cards.

\(P(\text{king or queen}) = \dfrac{15}{101}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Do you think that the probability of getting a queen was higher if none of the cards were dropped ? Justify your answer.
rows.context: A group of friends wanted to play cards with two identical packs together. While shuffling the cards, three cards are dropped. Rest of the cards are shuffled and one card is drawn at random. Assuming that the dropped cards were a queen of hearts, a ten of spades and an ace of clubs, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Yes.

With no card dropped, there are 104 cards, 8 of them queens: \(P(\text{queen}) = \dfrac{8}{104}\).

After the three cards are dropped, 101 cards remain, and the queen of hearts is gone, leaving 7 queens: \(P(\text{queen}) = \dfrac{7}{101}\).

\(\dfrac{8}{104} > \dfrac{7}{101}\), since \(8 \times 101 = 808 > 7 \times 104 = 728\).

So the probability of getting a queen was higher if none of the cards were dropped.

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: Find the probability that the drawn card is a jack. Compare it with the probability when none of the cards were dropped. In which case is the probability of getting a jack higher ?
rows.context: A group of friends wanted to play cards with two identical packs together. While shuffling the cards, three cards are dropped. Rest of the cards are shuffled and one card is drawn at random. Assuming that the dropped cards were a queen of hearts, a ten of spades and an ace of clubs, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
None of the dropped cards is a jack, so all 8 jacks remain among the \(2 \times 52 - 3 = 101\) cards.

\(P(\text{jack, cards dropped}) = \dfrac{8}{101}\), and \(P(\text{jack, no card dropped}) = \dfrac{8}{104}\).

The numerators are equal and \(101 < 104\), so \(\dfrac{8}{101} > \dfrac{8}{104}\).

The probability of getting a jack is higher when the three cards were dropped.

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Determine the total height of the fountain.
rows.context:
A model of Leafy Ball Fountain is made to be kept on the tabletop. Water gently cascades down the ball into a decorative cylindrical pool where it is recycled.

The diameter of spherical ball is 21 cm.

Cylindrical pool – Outer diameter is 50 cm and inner diameter is 40 cm.

Height of solid base is 14 cm.

Height of water filled is 7 cm.

Observe the figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - where the ball rests relative to the solid base and the water is shown only in the dimensioned drawing (heights 14 and 7 marked on the pool); the passage gives the sizes but not how the parts stack. The photograph of a garden ball fountain beside it is decorative. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
In the figure the ball rests on top of the 14 cm solid base, and its diameter is 21 cm.

Total height of the fountain \(= 14 + 21 = 35\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the volume of the ball.
rows.context:
A model of Leafy Ball Fountain is made to be kept on the tabletop. Water gently cascades down the ball into a decorative cylindrical pool where it is recycled.

The diameter of spherical ball is 21 cm.

Cylindrical pool – Outer diameter is 50 cm and inner diameter is 40 cm.

Height of solid base is 14 cm.

Height of water filled is 7 cm.

Observe the figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the ball in the pool; the ball's diameter is in the passage. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
The radius of the ball is \(\dfrac{21}{2}\) cm.

Volume of the ball \(= \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{21}{2} \times \dfrac{21}{2} \times \dfrac{21}{2} = 4851\ \text{cm}^3\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: If one-third of the ball is submerged in the water, find the volume of the water filled in the pool.
rows.context:
A model of Leafy Ball Fountain is made to be kept on the tabletop. Water gently cascades down the ball into a decorative cylindrical pool where it is recycled.

The diameter of spherical ball is 21 cm.

Cylindrical pool – Outer diameter is 50 cm and inner diameter is 40 cm.

Height of solid base is 14 cm.

Height of water filled is 7 cm.

Observe the figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the ball resting in 7 cm of water above the solid base; the inner diameter and water height are in the passage. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
The water fills the inner part of the pool above the base, a cylinder of radius \(\dfrac{40}{2} = 20\) cm and height 7 cm, except for the part of the ball under water. One-third of the ball is under water, and the ball's volume is \(\dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \left(\dfrac{21}{2}\right)^3 = 4851\ \text{cm}^3\).

Volume of water \(=\) volume of the inner upper part \(- \dfrac{1}{3} \times\) volume of the ball

\(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 20 \times 20 \times 7 - \dfrac{1}{3} \times 4851 = 8800 - 1617 = 7183\ \text{cm}^3\).

The one-third is given in the question and is used as it stands; it is not what the 7 cm depth of water would give geometrically.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the sum of the outer curved surface area of the cylindrical part and surface area of the ball.
rows.context:
A model of Leafy Ball Fountain is made to be kept on the tabletop. Water gently cascades down the ball into a decorative cylindrical pool where it is recycled.

The diameter of spherical ball is 21 cm.

Cylindrical pool – Outer diameter is 50 cm and inner diameter is 40 cm.

Height of solid base is 14 cm.

Height of water filled is 7 cm.

Observe the figure and answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the height of the cylindrical part's outer wall is not in the passage; it comes only from the heights marked on the drawing. Page idx 26.
rows.solution:
The cylindrical part has outer radius \(\dfrac{50}{2} = 25\) cm, and from the figure its outer wall rises \(14 + 7 = 21\) cm. The ball has radius \(\dfrac{21}{2}\) cm.

Required area \(=\) outer curved surface area of the cylindrical part \(+\) surface area of the ball

\(= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 25 \times 21 + 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{21}{2} \times \dfrac{21}{2} = 3300 + 1386 = 4686\ \text{cm}^2\).
